title: A Sky Full of Galaxies
caption: A field of galaxies including LEDA 14884, imaged by the Dark Energy Camera on the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope
credit: CTIO/NOIRLab/DOE/NSF/AURA. Image processing: Travis Rector (University of Alaska, Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), Jen Miller (Gemini Observatory/NSF NOIRLab), Mahdi Zamani & Davide de Martin (NSF NOIRLab)

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Bright dots scattered across black space make this look like a detailed photo of a star-filled night sky. It isn't. Although the image was taken from Earth's southern hemisphere, the dots are galaxies, and the distinctive ring-shaped one on the right is LEDA 14884.

The picture was assembled from Dark Energy Survey data. That ambitious project mapped hundreds of millions of galaxies using the Dark Energy Camera (DECam), a Department of Energy instrument that works on the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope in Chile.

Thousands of very different galaxies crowd a single field. Only about 100 years ago, though, most astronomers believed the Milky Way was the only galaxy there was. In 1925, Edwin Hubble, drawing on earlier work by Henrietta Leavitt and Ejnar Hertzsprung, demonstrated that the Andromeda Galaxy sits outside our own galaxy, and people began to grasp how vast the Universe really is.

understand.summary: Taken with DECam on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope through g, r and i filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
